sub_questions: What are the common types of prompt injection attacks in AI agents?
What role do guardrails play in safeguarding against prompt injection vulnerabilities in agent software?
What are the limitations of using guardrails to prevent prompt injection attacks?
report:
Question: Can guardrails alone prevent prompt injection in agents?

## s1. What are the common types of prompt injection attacks in AI agents?
- (supports) Direct prompt injection involves the attacker directly inputting malicious instructions. [doc-001]
- (supports) Indirect prompt injection involves the instruction being hidden in external content that the agent reads. [doc-001]
- (supports) MELON is a defense against indirect prompt injection in LLM agents. [doc-010]

## s2. What role do guardrails play in safeguarding against prompt injection vulnerabilities in agent software?
- (supports) No single control stops prompt injection, and layering defences is important. [doc-003]

## s3. What are the limitations of using guardrails to prevent prompt injection attacks?
- (supports) Guardrails alone cannot prevent prompt injection attacks. [doc-005]

Coverage: 3/3 sub-questions have verified evidence.

## Evidence table
| sub-question | source | stance | quote |
|---|---|---|---|
| s1 | doc-001 | supports | "Direct prompt injection happens when the attacker types the malicious instruction into the input the user controls." |
| s1 | doc-001 | supports | "Indirect prompt injection happens when the instruction is hidden in external content that the agent reads, such as a web page, a document or an email." |
| s1 | doc-010 | supports | "MELON is a defense against indirect prompt injection in LLM agents." |
| s2 | doc-003 | supports | "No single control stops prompt injection. Commonly combined defences are input and output filtering, privilege separation, human approval for sensitive actions, and treating retrieved content as data rather than instructions." |
| s3 | doc-005 | supports | "Critics argue that guardrails alone cannot prevent prompt injection. An adaptive attacker who can iterate on the wording can find inputs that a filter misses, and natural language has no fixed grammar that a filter can enumerate." |
